chunks: Making data persist after power-off. The question: What if I want memory to persist after the microcontroller powers off?
To keep data after power-off, you write it into non-volatile memory, such as EEPROM, flash, or FRAM. The memory is only part of the problem.
These memories wear out after a limited number of writes, and a power cut in the middle of a write can leave a half-written record. Good designs plan for both.
Imagine a notebook written in pencil. Each page can be erased and rewritten only so many times before it tears. So you rotate through many pages instead of rewriting one.
If the lights go out while you are writing a sentence, you are left with half a sentence. So you keep the old page until the new one is finished and checked.
Boot-time recovery. A torn write fails its CRC and is ignored, and the previous record (lower sequence number) is still intact, so you lose at most the last update.
Non-volatile: ("What non-volatile memory means"): keeps its contents without power. Endurance: how many times a memory can be written and erased before it may fail.
Wear leveling: spreading writes over many locations so none wears out early. FRAM: a non-volatile memory that survives a vast number of writes, around trillions.
CRC: a short check number calculated from the data. If it does not match, the record is corrupt.
A memory cell is rated for 1 million writes. You save one byte every second in the same place. It wears out after 1,000,000 seconds, about 11. 6 days.
Now rotate through 256 locations. Each one is written only once per 256 seconds, so the memory lasts 256 times longer, about 8 years.
Each record also gets a CRC and a version number, so after a power cut you can tell which copy is the good one. That is the whole idea.
"I'd store it in non-volatile memory: on-chip flash or EEPROM for settings, FRAM for data that changes constantly, and external flash or SD for large data.
A coin-cell backup domain can keep a clock and a few bytes alive too.
The important part is robustness: respect the endurance limit with wear levelling, and protect against power loss mid-write using CRCs, sequence numbers and alternating slots."
